a: Wisdom
p: In chapter 10 Wisdom guided the righteous from Adam to the Exodus. Here she acts once more, through Moses.
b: The verb has no named subject in the Greek: it simply goes on from chapter 10, where sophia, "wisdom", is the one who rescues the righteous from Adam to the crossing of the sea. The Plain names her and writes a capital W, because she acts as a person here: she "made their works succeed". This is the last time she drives the story. From 11:4 the speaker turns to God himself ("you"), and from here on it is God who acts in the Exodus. She is named as a person once more, "Wisdom, the craftswoman", whose skill builds ships (14:2; see the note there). The rule is the same through the whole book: a capital W where she acts or is described as a person, a small w where the word means a quality, as in "the works of your wisdom" (14:5). The verse is the seam between the praise of wisdom (6–10) and the long retelling of the Exodus (11–19).
orig: Εὐόδωσεν (euodōsen), "she made prosper"

a: a holy prophet
p: The book never names Moses, but calls him a prophet, as Hosea and Deuteronomy do.
b: Wisdom of Solomon names no one in its history: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Joseph and Moses are all "a righteous man" or the like (chapter 10). Here Moses is "a holy prophet". The Hebrew Bible also calls him a prophet: "by a prophet the LORD brought Israel up out of Egypt" (Hosea 12:13), and Deuteronomy promises a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15; Deuteronomy 34:10). For Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria, Moses was the lawgiver and prophet whom Philo celebrated in his Life of Moses. Leaving the names out lets the readers fill them in, and turns the story into a pattern: how God treats the righteous and the ungodly at any time.

a: out of a sheer rock water was given to them
p: The Greek words come from Deuteronomy 8:15 in the Septuagint: water "from the sheer rock".
b: Twice in the wilderness Moses struck a rock and water came out: at Horeb (Exodus 17:6) and at Kadesh (Numbers 20:11). The Greek phrase ek petras akrotomou, "out of a sheer (or flinty) rock", is the very phrase of the Septuagint at Deuteronomy 8:15, where the Hebrew says "He brought water out of the flint rock for you" (Deuteronomy 8:15). Psalm 114:8 in Greek uses the same rare adjective. Wisdom of Solomon passes over the people's complaining at the rock (Exodus 17:3; Numbers 20:2) and makes the scene a prayer: "they called on you". Paul later reads the rock as the Christ who went with Israel (1 Corinthians 10:4).
orig: ἐκ πέτρας ἀκροτόμου (ek petras akrotomou)

a: The very things that punished their enemies
p: The rest of the book is built on this rule: what struck Egypt saved Israel.
b: This verse states the plan of the rest of the book. Through chapters 11–19 the writer sets out a series of contrasts (this site counts seven): water (11:6–14), animals (16:1–4), more animals (16:5–14), the hail and the manna (16:15–29), darkness and light (17:1–18:4), the death of the firstborn (18:5–25) and the sea (19:1–9). In each, one and the same part of God's creation punishes Egypt and blesses Israel. The first contrast fits the pattern closely: Egypt's river turned to blood (Exodus 7:20–21), while Israel drank from the rock. Two digressions interrupt the series: one on God's mercy (11:15–12:27) and one on idols (13–15).

a: as a rebuke for the order to kill the babies
p: The writer ties the first plague to Pharaoh's order to drown Israel's baby boys in the Nile.
b: Pharaoh ordered: "Every son who is born, you must throw into the Nile" (Exodus 1:22). Exodus does not link that order to the first plague, when "The blood was everywhere in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 7:21). Wisdom of Solomon does: the river that swallowed the babies became blood. It is an early example of the rule the book will soon state in 11:16. The chapter page on Exodus 7 on this site discusses the same link. The Greek nēpioktonou diatagmatos means "the baby-killing decree".

a: like a father who warns
p: God disciplines Israel as a father and condemns Egypt as a stern king.
b: Two pictures of God stand side by side: the father who warns (noutheteō) and the harsh (apotomos) king who condemns. Israel is God's son in Exodus: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), and Deuteronomy says that "the LORD your God trains you the way a man trains his son" (Deuteronomy 8:5). The same contrast returns in 12:22. Compare what Hebrews 12:5–11 says about the Lord's discipline of his children.
orig: ὡς πατὴρ νουθετῶν (hōs patēr nouthetōn)

a: Whether they were away or close by
p: The Greek does not name them. Most likely "they" are the Egyptians, near Israel or far away.
b: The Greek says only "being absent and being present". The likeliest reading takes the Egyptians as the subject: whether Israel was still among them or had gone, they suffered alike, first from the plague, then from grief and envy when they heard (11:12–13) that the Israelites had water in the desert. The KJV keeps the ambiguity ("Whether they were absent or present"). The Plain keeps it too.
orig: ἀπόντες δὲ καὶ παρόντες (apontes de kai parontes)

a: cast out as a baby to die
p: The writer calls the basket on the Nile an "exposure", the Greek word for leaving a baby to die.
b: The Greek ekthesis was the ordinary word for the exposure of unwanted infants, a common practice in the Greek world. Exodus tells that Moses' mother "laid the child in it and placed it in the reeds by the bank of the Nile" (Exodus 2:3), because Pharaoh's decree had ordered such boys thrown into the river (Exodus 1:22). The Greek verb is passive, "the one cast out long ago", and does not say who cast him out; read with the decree, the blame falls on Egypt. The Egyptians later mocked him and turned him away (Exodus 5:2–4), and at the end they were amazed at him (Exodus 11:3). The KJV places the last line of this verse ("thirsting in another manner than the just") at the end of 11:9, following an older way of dividing the verses.
orig: ἐν ἐκθέσει πάλαι ῥιφέντα (en ekthesei palai rhiphenta)

a: mindless reptiles and worthless vermin
p: Egyptians honored many animals as sacred. Jewish writers in Egypt mocked this.
b: Egyptian religion honored gods in animal form and kept sacred animals: bulls, crocodiles, ibises, hawks, snakes and others. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of the same city a little later, scorns the Egyptians for giving "the honours due to the gods" to "irrational animals" such as bulls, rams and goats, and also lions, crocodiles, the asp, dogs, ibises and hawks (Philo, On the Decalogue 76–79). Wisdom of Solomon uses the same word, aloga, "without reason". The frogs, gnats and flies of the plagues (Exodus 8) are, for this writer, the fitting punishment: mindless animals for those who worshiped mindless animals. The theme returns in 12:24 and 15:18–19.
orig: ἄλογα ἑρπετὰ καὶ κνώδαλα εὐτελῆ (aloga herpeta kai knōdala eutelē)

a: what a person sins with, he is punished with
p: The rule that the punishment fits the sin: Jewish, Greek and Christian writers all used it.
b: The rule runs through the Bible's stories. Psalm 7:15–16 says the one who digs a pit falls into it; Haman hangs on his own pole (Esther 7:10). The Mishnah puts it as a saying: "With the measure that a person measures, he is measured with it" (Mishnah Sotah 1:7), and Jesus says, "The measure you use is the one that will be used to measure out to you" (Matthew 7:2). Here it explains the plagues of animals. It can be taken two ways: as a law of fitting punishment built into the world, or as a sign of God's mercy, since a punishment that matches the sin teaches the sinner what he did (11:23; 12:2). The writer leans to the second.
orig: δι᾽ ὧν τις ἁμαρτάνει, διὰ τούτων κολάζεται (di' hōn tis hamartanei, dia toutōn kolazetai)

a: out of formless matter
p: The writer uses a Greek philosopher's phrase for creation. Did he mean God shaped matter that was already there?
b: The Greek ex amorphou hylēs is a term from Greek philosophy: hylē is "matter", and amorphos "without form". In Plato's Timaeus a divine craftsman orders a formless stuff into a world. The Septuagint of Genesis 1:2 says the earth was "invisible and unformed" (aoratos kai akataskeuastos), and the Plain of Genesis 1:2 says "The earth was shapeless and empty". So the phrase may mean only the shapeless earth of Genesis 1:2, which God then formed. Or it may mean that matter existed before God made the world, as Plato taught. 2 Maccabees 7:28 says God made the world "not from things that were", and the churches' answers on creation from nothing are on the card at 2 Maccabees 7. The writer's point here is power: the hand that formed the world could easily have sent lions.
orig: ἐξ ἀμόρφου ὕλης (ex amorphou hylēs)

a: or blowing out foul-smelling smoke
p: The Greek bromos can mean a roar or a stink. The KJV says "filthy scents".
b: The Greek bromous likmōmenous kapnou is hard. Bromos usually means a roar or crackling noise, but a word spelled almost the same, brōmos, means a stink, and the KJV took it so ("filthy scents of scattered smoke"). Likmaō is to winnow, to scatter as chaff. The Plain follows the sense the KJV gives, since beasts are blowing out smoke; "roaring" is possible too. Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi have the singular bromon (Swete's apparatus), which does not settle the choice between the two senses. The point is the same: God could have invented new monsters, like the fire-breathing creature of Job 41:19–21, but he did not.
orig: βρόμους λικμωμένους καπνοῦ (bromous likmōmenous kapnou)

a: hunted down
p: The Greek dikē was also the name of the Greek goddess of justice. Here it is God's justice at work.
b: Greek readers knew Dikē, Justice, as a divine figure who pursued wrongdoers. Here the wicked could have been "pursued" (diōchthentes) by her. The book makes her an agent elsewhere too: in 1:8 Justice presses her charge against anyone who speaks wickedly, and in 14:31 the same word, there translated "the penalty" that sinners have earned, "pursues" the wrongdoing of the unrighteous. The Plain writes a capital J where the Greek makes her a person (1:8 and here), as it does for Wisdom; she acts only by God's power ("the breath of your power").
orig: ὑπὸ τῆς δίκης διωχθέντες (hypo tēs dikēs diōchthentes)

a: by measure, by number and by weight
p: One of the book's most quoted lines. Augustine used it for the order of creation.
b: The writer means that God holds back: his punishments are measured, not unlimited. But the line came to mean much more. Augustine quotes it in The City of God (11.30), right after explaining why six is a perfect number and why God finished creation in six days: numbers, he says, belong among God's praises. Compare Isaiah 40:12, where the LORD weighs the mountains, and Job 28:25.
orig: μέτρῳ καὶ ἀριθμῷ καὶ σταθμῷ (metrō kai arithmō kai stathmō)

a: like the slight weight that tips a pair of scales
p: The two pictures come from Isaiah 40:15 in Greek: a drop and a turn of the scale.
b: Isaiah says the nations are "a drop dripping from a bucket, / no more than dust on a pair of scales" (Isaiah 40:15). The Septuagint there has rhopē zygou, "the turn of a balance", the tiny weight that tips it, and Wisdom of Solomon uses the same word rhopē. Isaiah's point is the nations' smallness; this writer turns it toward mercy: because the world is so small before God, he has no need to crush it (11:23).
orig: ὡς ῥοπὴ ἐκ πλαστίγγων (hōs rhopē ek plastingōn)

a: you show mercy to all
p: The writer argues that God's power is the reason for his mercy, not a limit on it.
b: Many would expect "because you can do all things, you punish". The writer says the reverse: God shows mercy because he is all-powerful. He has nothing to fear and nothing to prove (12:16–18). The Catholic Church reads 11:22–12:2 on the 31st Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year C, alongside the story of Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1–10), the rich man Jesus seeks out. The verse recalls God's own words in Exodus 34:6–7, and Jonah's complaint, "I knew that you are a God gracious and compassionate" (Jonah 4:2).

a: You look past people's sins
p: Paul uses the same idea: God looked past "those times of not knowing" and now calls everyone to repent.
b: The Greek paroraō means "look past, overlook". Paul tells the Athenians, "God has looked past those times of not knowing" (Acts 17:30), with the verb hyperidōn, and says that God now tells all people everywhere to repent, and he warns the Romans not to make light of God's kindness, which "is leading you to repentance" (Romans 2:4). 2 Peter 3:9 says the Lord "wants all to arrive at repentance". In Wisdom of Solomon the delay has a purpose: "to bring them to repentance" (literally "toward repentance").
orig: παρορᾷς ἁμαρτήματα ἀνθρώπων εἰς μετάνοιαν (paroras hamartēmata anthrōpōn eis metanoian)

a: You love all that is
p: Thomas Aquinas quotes this verse: God hates nothing he made.
b: The verse is one of the strongest statements in the Greek Old Testament of God's love for everything that exists. Genesis says God saw everything he had made, "and there it was, very good" (Genesis 1:31). The argument is short: to make something is to want it; so God, who made all things, cannot hate them. The writer will still say God "hated" the Canaanites for their deeds (12:4), so he means God's love for what he made, not approval of what people do. Thomas Aquinas quotes it to show that God loves all things that exist (Summa Theologiae I, question 20, article 2, where the Latin Bible numbers the verse 11:25).

a: Master, lover of souls
p: The Greek philopsychos means one who loves life, or loves souls: God cares for every living thing.
b: Philopsychos is built from philo-, "loving", and psychē, "soul, life". Here it is said of God: he loves psychai, souls, that is, living beings. The site renders psychē "soul" throughout this book, and here it has its wide sense of everything that lives. "Master" is Despota, the title of a lord over servants (see terms). In 12:19 the righteous are told to be philanthrōpos, "loving people": God's love for living things is the model for theirs.
orig: Δέσποτα φιλόψυχε (Despota philopsyche)

a: Your imperishable spirit is in everything
t: Compared with the Bible: God's spirit in all things
p: The Bible says God's Spirit is everywhere and gives life. This verse says it in words that sound Stoic.
b: Agrees with the Bible that God's Spirit is present everywhere and is the life of creation (Psalm 104:30; Psalm 139:7); the writer has already said that the Lord's spirit fills the world (1:7). Goes beyond it in its wording. The Stoics taught that a divine breath (pneuma) runs through the whole world and holds it together, and the writer uses that kind of language: God's "imperishable spirit" is in all things, as Wisdom passes through all things (7:24). He never says the spirit is the world, as a Stoic might; God remains the Master (11:26) who cares for each thing. The term "imperishable" (aphthartos) is the book's key word for what does not decay (2:23).
orig: τὸ γὰρ ἄφθαρτὸν σου πνεῦμά (to gar aphtharton sou pneuma)

a: a little at a time
p: The phrase returns in 12:8 and 12:10. Exodus and Deuteronomy said God would drive out the Canaanites "bit by bit".
b: The Greek kat' oligon (here) and kata brachy (12:8, 12:10) both mean "a little at a time". Exodus gives a practical reason for the slow conquest: "Bit by bit I will drive them out ahead of you" so that the wild animals would not take over (Exodus 23:30; Deuteronomy 7:22). Wisdom of Solomon gives a moral reason: the slowness was mercy, a chance to repent. This is one of the earliest Jewish answers to the moral problem of the conquest of Canaan.
orig: κατ᾽ ὀλίγον (kat' oligon)

a: your holy land
p: An early use of "holy land" for the whole country. In the Hebrew Bible it appears only at Zechariah 2:12.
b: "The holy land" for Canaan as a whole is rare in the Bible. The Hebrew has it once, at Zechariah 2:12 (the "soil of holiness"; see the note there on this site). Wisdom of Solomon has it here and calls it "the land you prize above all others" (12:7). For Jews living in Egypt, far from Judea, the land was still God's own, the place of the temple.
orig: τῆς ἁγίας σου γῆς (tēs hagias sou gēs)

a: acts of sorcery and unholy rites
p: The writer lists the sins the Torah gives as reasons for the conquest, and adds charges in the words of Greek cults.
b: Deuteronomy forbids anyone "who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire, anyone who practices divination, reads signs, looks for omens or works sorcery" (Deuteronomy 18:10) and says that for such things the LORD drives the nations out. Leviticus 18:21–25 links child sacrifice to the land vomiting out its people, and Psalm 106:37–38 laments that Israel itself copied it. The charge of cannibal feasts and of "initiates" of a cult band (12:5) is not in the Hebrew Bible. Its words come from the Greek mystery cults: mystai are initiates, and a thiasos is a band of worshipers.
orig: ἔργα φαρμακειῶν καὶ τελετὰς ἀνοσίους (erga pharmakeiōn kai teletas anosious)

a: merciless murders of children
p: The Bible charges Canaan and, later, Israel with offering children.
b: The Hebrew Bible repeatedly condemns making children "pass through the fire" (Deuteronomy 18:10; Leviticus 18:21) and blames Israel's kings for it (2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6). Wisdom of Solomon makes it the first crime of the old inhabitants. The writer is retelling the Torah's charge, not reporting new evidence. See the molech topic.

a: a worthy colony of God's children
p: The Greek paides can mean children or servants. The book uses it both ways.
b: Paides theou could be "God's servants" or "God's children". The same word stands at 2:13, where the ungodly mock the righteous man for calling himself pais kyriou, and in Isaiah's Greek for the Servant of the Lord. Here the Plain says "children", as 12:19–21 goes on to speak of God's "children" and "sons" (huioi). The word apoikia, "colony", is the Greek word for a settlement sent out from a mother city: the writer pictures Israel's arrival in Canaan the way Greeks pictured the founding of a colony.
orig: ἀποικίαν δέξηται θεοῦ παίδων (apoikian dexētai theou paidōn)

a: You sent wasps
p: Hebrew tsir'ah is usually "hornet". The Septuagint and Wisdom say "wasps".
b: Exodus promises, "I will send the hornet in front of you" (Exodus 23:28; compare Deuteronomy 7:20 and Joshua 24:12). The Hebrew word tsir'ah is rare and debated: an insect, or a figure for panic or for Egypt. The Septuagint in Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20 has sphēkiai, a kind of wasp, and Wisdom of Solomon has sphēkes, "wasps". The writer takes them as real insects and as "forerunners of your army", scouts sent ahead of Israel's troops. The point is again restraint: God used something small to drive the people out slowly.
orig: προδρόμους τοῦ στρατοπέδου σου σφῆκας (prodromous tou stratopedou sou sphēkas)

a: gave them room for repentance
p: Hebrews 12:17 uses the same two Greek words of Esau, who found no room for repentance.
b: The Greek topon metanoias, literally "a place of repentance", uses the same two words as Hebrews 12:17, in the opposite order (metanoias topon), where Esau "found no place for repentance, though he searched for it with tears" (Hebrews 12:17). In Wisdom of Solomon God gives this "place" even to peoples whose wickedness was "born in them", which raises the question the next verse answers: why give time to those who will not change?
orig: ἐδίδους τόπον μετανοίας (edidous topon metanoias)

a: that their wickedness was born in them
t: Compared with the Bible: a cursed race?
p: Genesis curses Canaan, and the Torah blames the Canaanites for their deeds. This verse says their evil was inborn.
b: Agrees with the Torah that the Canaanites' guilt was real and was given time to grow: "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16), and Noah says, "A curse on Canaan!" (Genesis 9:25). Goes beyond the Hebrew Bible in saying their evil was "inborn" (emphytos) and that they were "a seed cursed from the beginning" (12:11), which sounds as if a whole people were wicked by birth. The Torah grounds the judgment in what the peoples did (Leviticus 18:24–25; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), and warns Israel that the land will treat it the same way. The verse can be read two ways: the writer may speak of a long-hardened culture, not of individuals; or he here goes further than the Bible does. Note that he still says God gave them room to repent.

a: Who will say, "What have you done?"
t: No one can call God to account
p: The question comes from Job and returns in Paul's argument in Romans 9.
b: Job says of God, "Who will ask him, 'What are you doing?'" (Job 9:12), and Ecclesiastes 8:4 and Daniel 4:35 ask the same of a king and of God. Paul uses the argument in Romans 9: "No, human being, who are you to argue against God?" (Romans 9:20), and goes on to the potter, like Wisdom of Solomon 15:7. Here the point is not that God may do what he likes, but that God's judgment needs no defense because it was already patient and fair (12:15).

a: Your strength is where righteousness begins
p: Some Greek thinkers in Plato's dialogues said might makes right. This writer turns the saying around.
b: In Plato's Republic Thrasymachus says that justice is "the advantage of the stronger" (book 1, 338c), and in the Gorgias Callicles argues that nature shows "it is right for the better to have advantage of the worse" (483d). Wisdom of Solomon also joins power and righteousness in God, but the other way around: because God is all-powerful, he has nothing to gain by injustice, so his rule is fair and sparing (12:15–18). The word archē can mean "beginning", "source" or "rule". The Catholic lectionary reads 12:13 and 12:16–19 on the 16th Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year A, with the parable of the weeds, where the master lets both grow until the harvest (Matthew 13:24–30).
orig: ἡ γὰρ ἰσχύς σου δικαιοσύνης ἀρχή (hē gar ischys sou dikaiosynēs archē)

a: that whoever is righteous must love people
p: The Greek philanthrōpos, "loving people", was a royal virtue in the Greek world. Here God teaches it to Israel.
b: Philanthrōpos, "humane, loving people", was praised in Greek kings and was a favorite virtue in Hellenistic writing. Wisdom herself is called philanthrōpon in 1:6 and 7:23. Here the lesson goes from God to his people: as God was gentle with his enemies, the righteous must be kind to all. Titus 3:4 uses the noun of God: "when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for humankind appeared" (Titus 3:4). The verse shows the book's aim: Israel's history is meant to shape how Israel treats others.
orig: δεῖ τὸν δίκαιον εἶναι φιλάνθρωπον (dei ton dikaion einai philanthrōpon)

a: you whip our enemies ten thousand times as hard
t: Discipline for us, scourging for them
p: Israel is disciplined; its enemies are punished far more. 2 Maccabees makes a similar contrast.
b: The verse draws the lesson of the chapter: Israel is disciplined (paideuō) as children are, while its enemies are whipped (mastigoō) "ten thousand times" over. 2 Maccabees 6:12–16 makes a similar contrast: God punishes his people quickly so their sins do not pile up, but lets the nations' sins reach full measure. The aim is twofold: when Israel judges others, it should remember God's goodness; when Israel is judged, it should hope for mercy. Paul turns a similar thought against anyone who judges others (Romans 2:1–4).
orig: ἐν μυριότητι μαστιγοῖς (en myriotēti mastigois)

a: the most worthless even of hateful animals
p: The Greek tōn echthrōn can mean "hateful" animals or animals "of their enemies".
b: The phrase ta kai en zōois tōn echthrōn atima is hard. If echthrōn is an adjective, it means "the most despised even among hateful animals", which matches 15:18, "the most hateful animals" (ta echthista). If it is a noun, it means "animals that even their enemies despise", that is, creatures the Israelites themselves scorned, and the KJV reads it so ("which even among the beasts of their enemies were despised"). The Plain follows the first reading for its match with 15:18.
orig: τὰ καὶ ἐν ζῴοις τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἄτιμα (ta kai en zōois tōn echthrōn atima)

a: they now recognized as the true God
p: In Exodus God acts "so that Egypt will know that I am the LORD". The writer says Egypt did know, too late.
b: Exodus repeats that the plagues and the sea were meant so that "Egypt will know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 14:4; Exodus 7:5). Wisdom of Solomon says the Egyptians did come to know: suffering through the very animals they worshiped, they recognized the true God. Yet knowing did not change them, and "the final sentence" came at the sea (19:1–4). The writer will make the same charge against the nature-worshipers in 13:8–9: they knew enough to find God and did not.

a: All people were empty by nature
p: The Greek mataioi means futile, empty. "By nature" may mean by birth or simply "utterly".
b: Mataios is "vain, futile, empty", the word the Septuagint uses for idols and for the "vanity" of Ecclesiastes (mataiotēs). Physei, "by nature", is debated: either all people are born empty-headed unless they come to know God, or it means simply "empty in their very nature, utterly". Paul says the Gentiles' "reasoning came to nothing" (Romans 1:21), where the Greek verb is from the same root. The Plain keeps "by nature".
orig: Μάταιοι μὲν γὰρ πάντες ἄνθρωποι φύσει (mataioi men gar pantes anthrōpoi physei)

a: the One Who Is
p: The name echoes the Greek of Exodus 3:14, where God says, "I am the One Who Is".
b: Where the Hebrew of Exodus 3:14 has "I will be who I will be" (Exodus 3:14), the Septuagint has Egō eimi ho ōn, "I am the One Who Is". Wisdom of Solomon uses the same participle, ton onta, so that the God the nations should have found in nature is the God of Moses. Greek philosophers also spoke of true Being as "that which is", so the name could speak to readers of Moses and of the philosophers alike.
orig: εἰδέναι τὸν ὄντα (eidenai ton onta)

a: the Craftsman
p: The Greek technitēs, "craftsman", is the masculine of technitis, Wisdom's title in 7:22. Hebrews 11:10 uses it of God.
b: Technitēs is an artisan, a skilled worker. Wisdom is called the craftswoman (technitis, the feminine form) of all things in 7:22, and again in 8:6 and 14:2; in Proverbs she says, "I was at his side, a craftsman" (Proverbs 8:30). Hebrews uses technitēs of God: "the city whose architect and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:10), where the site's Hebrews renders the same word "architect". In 13:1–9 the argument is the craftsman's: from a beautiful work, you should know there is a maker. Chapter 13 then shows human craftsmen (13:11) making what is not God.
orig: τὸν τεχνίτην (ton technitēn)

a: fire, or wind, or quick-moving air
p: Greek thinkers made the elements divine. Jewish writers in Alexandria attacked this.
b: The list is the Greek world's: fire, wind (pneuma), air, the circle of the stars, water, and "the lights of heaven" (the sun and moon). Greek philosophers named the elements as the stuff of the world, and some, like the Stoics, called fire or the world itself divine. Philo reports that some nations made gods of the four elements and others worshiped the sun, moon, planets and fixed stars (Philo, On the Decalogue 53), and that people gave the elements gods' names: in the old English translation, the sea is Neptune, the air Juno and fire Vulcan (54), the Latin names for Poseidon, Hera and Hephaestus. "The lights" (phōstēres) is the Septuagint word for the sun and moon in Genesis 1:14, so the writer reminds his readers that these were made on the fourth day. Galatians 4:3 and 4:9 may speak of the same "elements".
orig: φωστῆρας οὐρανοῦ πρυτάνεις κόσμου (phōstēras ouranou prytaneis kosmou)

a: their Maker is seen, by analogy
p: The Greek analogōs means "in proportion". From it came the theological term "analogy".
b: Analogōs is a word from Greek mathematics: "in proportion, correspondingly". As the work is great and beautiful, so, in proportion, is its maker. Christian teachers later used "analogy" for how words can be said both of creatures and of God. Thomas Aquinas teaches that names are said of God and creatures "in an analogous sense, i.e. according to proportion" (Summa Theologiae I, question 13, article 5); that article cites Romans 1:20, not this verse, so the link between the two is this site's observation. The Catholic Catechism does quote 13:5 when it says that creatures' perfections let us name God (Catechism 41), and John of Damascus cites the verse at the start of his Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith (1.1). See the card on this chapter.
orig: ἀναλόγως ὁ γενεσιουργὸς αὐτῶν θεωρεῖται (analogōs ho genesiourgos autōn theōreitai)

a: From how great and how beautiful created things are
p: Paul's argument in Romans 1:19–25 runs close to this chapter, step by step.
b: Paul says that God's "unseen qualities, his everlasting power and divine nature, are visible to the mind in what he has made. This leaves them with no defense" (Romans 1:20). The steps match Wisdom 13: God is known from creation (13:1–5); people are without excuse (13:8); they turn to idols, "an image of mortal man, of birds, of four-footed animals and of crawling things" (Romans 1:23; Wisdom 13:10–14:21); vice follows (Romans 1:24–31; Wisdom 14:22–27). The texts alone do not show whether Paul had read this book or drew on the same synagogue teaching; the note at Romans 1:20 on this site speaks of a way of arguing familiar in Jewish synagogues. There is a difference: Wisdom of Solomon goes on to exempt "us" (15:2–4), while Paul turns at once to say that the one who judges does the same things (Romans 2:1). See the notes at Romans 1:20 and Romans 2:1 on this site.

a: while they search for God and long to find him
t: Compared with the Bible: how much blame?
p: Wisdom calls the nature-worshipers' blame small. Paul says they hold down the truth.
b: Agrees with the New Testament that people may seek God through his works: Paul tells the Athenians that God made them "so that they would look for God, in the hope that they might grope for him and find him" (Acts 17:27), and says at Lystra that God "did not leave himself without a witness" (Acts 14:17). It also agrees that such seekers have no excuse: "even they are not to be excused" (13:8; compare Romans 1:20). Partly in tension with Romans 1: Wisdom of Solomon calls their blame "small", since they were seeking God, while Paul says they "hold down the truth by their unrighteousness" (Romans 1:18). The writer is gentler with nature-worshipers than with idol-makers (13:10); Romans 1 draws no such line. Acts 17:29 takes this chapter's next step: "we should not suppose that the Divine looks like gold or silver or stone" (Acts 17:29).

a: explore the world
p: The Greek aiōn usually means "age" or "eternity". Here it seems to mean the universe.
b: Stochasasthai ton aiōna literally means "to aim at (or guess at) the aiōn". Aiōn often means "age, lifetime, eternity", and it could be read so here: "to speculate about eternity". But here it seems to mean the world as a whole, the universe that the philosophers studied, and the KJV says "aim at the world". The argument is sharp: if their minds could reach so far, they could have reached its Master.
orig: στοχάσασθαι τὸν αἰῶνα (stochasasthai ton aiōna)

a: a useless stone carved by some hand long ago
p: An old statue of unknown origin might be honored just for its age.
b: Greek temples kept ancient images, some said to have fallen from heaven, like the image of Artemis at Ephesus that the town clerk mentions (Acts 19:35). The writer sneers: it is only a stone, and some forgotten hand made it. The verse begins the attack on images made by hand (13:10–15:17), which follows the Hebrew prophets, Isaiah 44:9–20, Jeremiah 10:1–16 and Psalm 115:4–8.

a: He burns the scraps from his work to cook his food
p: The scene retells Isaiah 44: the same wood cooks a meal and becomes a god.
b: Isaiah mocks a man who uses a tree for fuel and for a god: "Half the wood he burns in the fire. / Over that half he cooks meat to eat" and "What is left he turns into a god, his idol" (Isaiah 44:16–17). Wisdom of Solomon sharpens the joke: the useful part becomes furniture, the scraps feed the fire, and the god is made from the one piece that is good for nothing, carved in his spare time. The tone is like a Greek satire, but the argument is the prophet's.

a: since it is an image and has to be helped
p: The idol must be nailed up so it will not fall. Isaiah and Jeremiah make the same joke.
b: The writer piles up the irony: the maker has to "see to it that it does not fall over" and fasten it with iron (13:15). Isaiah says idol-makers make an idol "strong with nails, so it will not tip over" (Isaiah 41:7), and Jeremiah says, "Someone always has to pick them up, for they take no steps" (Jeremiah 10:5). The contrast is with the God who helps (14:3–4), and who in Isaiah 46:3–4 carries his people instead of being carried.

a: for a good journey he asks what cannot even take a step
p: Each prayer asks for what the idol most obviously lacks: life, health, help, travel, strength.
b: The list is built so that every request meets its opposite: health from the weak, life from the dead, help from what knows nothing, a journey from what cannot step, success for the hands from what has no working hands. Psalm 115 says idols have feet but "with their feet they cannot walk" (Psalm 115:7) and adds, "The ones who make them will end up like them" (Psalm 115:8). Habakkuk asks, "Can it teach?" (Habakkuk 2:19).

a: cries for help to a piece of wood
p: Ancient ships carried images of protecting gods. The writer contrasts them with God's providence.
b: Ancient ships often carried a small image of a protecting god, and their names could be gods' names: Acts 28:11 mentions a ship whose emblem was "the Twins, the sons of Zeus" (Acts 28:11), Castor and Pollux, the sailors' gods. The writer's joke: the sailor prays to wood more rotten than the wood of his ship. Codex Alexandrinus even reads "more rotten than the wood that carries him" (see the variant).

a: Wisdom, the craftswoman
p: The same title as in 7:22: Wisdom is the craftswoman behind the shipbuilder's skill.
b: The Greek technitis sophia uses the feminine word for a craftsworker, the title Wisdom bears in 7:22 ("Wisdom, who crafted all things") and 8:6. So the Plain writes a capital W here: the skill that builds a ship is her work, as in 10:4 she piloted the ark. The same chapter keeps a small w for God's wisdom as a quality, "the works of your wisdom" (14:5). The point is that every part of a voyage, the trade that plans it and the skill that builds the ship, comes from God, so the sailor has no reason to pray to a scrap of wood.
orig: τεχνῖτις δὲ σοφία (technitis de sophia)

a: your providence, Father
p: This is one of the first Jewish texts to call God's care "providence", a Greek philosophical word.
b: Pronoia, "forethought", was the Stoics' word for the divine reason that governs the world. The writer takes it over for the God of Israel (also 17:2). He also calls God "Father" in direct address, which is rare before the New Testament; compare "You, LORD, are our Father" (Isaiah 63:16) and Sirach 23:1 and 23:4. The steering picture (diakybernaō) is the language of a helmsman. The road in the sea recalls Isaiah 43:16, "who opened a road in the sea" (Isaiah 43:16), which the Septuagint gives in words very close to these.
orig: ἡ δὲ σή, πάτερ, διακυβερνᾷ πρόνοια (hē de sē, pater, diakybernai pronoia)

a: people hand over their souls to the tiniest scrap of wood
p: Psychē here is "life": sailors trust their lives to a small boat.
b: The site renders psychē "soul" throughout Wisdom of Solomon, because the book cares about the soul's survival (3:1). Here the word has its common sense of "life": sailors risk their lives in a small boat. 1 Peter 3:20 uses it the same way of the ark: "a few, eight souls, were carried safe through water". The writer is preparing for the ark in the next verse.
orig: ἐλαχίστῳ ξύλῳ πιστεύουσιν ἄνθρωποι ψυχάς (elachistō xylō pisteuousin anthrōpoi psychas)

a: when the proud giants were dying
p: The writer links the Flood to the giants of Genesis 6:4, as 1 Enoch and other Jewish books do.
b: Genesis 6:4 mentions the Nephilim, "the heroes of ancient times", just before the Flood, and the Septuagint calls them gigantes, "giants". Several Jewish writings of this period tell of their pride and their end: Sirach 16:7 says God did not forgive the ancient giants who rebelled in their strength, Baruch 3:26–28 says they perished for lack of understanding, 3 Maccabees 2:4 says God destroyed them with a flood of water, and 1 Enoch tells their story at length (1 Enoch 7; 1 Enoch 10). Wisdom of Solomon shares the tradition but adds nothing about angels: the giants are "proud", and the ark, a mere raft, carried "the hope of the world". Noah, again unnamed (10:4), is the seed of a new humanity.
r: Genesis 6:4; Genesis 7:23; 10:4; Sirach 16:7; Baruch 3:26–28; 1 Enoch 7; 3 Maccabees 2:4; 2 Peter 2:5

a: For blessed is wood through which righteousness comes about
p: The writer means Noah's ark. A bishop quoted by John of Damascus read the line of the cross.
b: In context the "wood" is the ark (14:6), through which righteous Noah was saved and the world began again, set against the cursed wood of the idol (14:8). Hebrews says Noah through the ark "came to inherit the righteousness that matches faith" (Hebrews 11:7). One Christian text reads the verse of the cross. John of Damascus, in his defense of the holy images, quotes "Leo, Bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus", from a book against the Jews on the honor given to the cross: after Moses' staff, which struck Pharaoh, parted the sea and drew water from the rock, he adds, "And Solomon said, 'Blessed is the wood by which justice cometh'". This is the only such witness this site has opened. In its own setting the verse speaks of the ark; the reading of the cross is a Christian application made from its words.
orig: εὐλόγηται γὰρ ξύλον δι᾽ οὗ γίνεται δικαιοσύνη (eulogētai gar xylon di' hou ginetai dikaiosynē)

a: blessed is wood
t: Claude's theory: blessed wood and cursed wood
p: My suggestion: chapters 13–14 build a contrast of woods, which a Christian reading later mapped onto the cross.
b: This is my own reading. From 13:11 to 14:8 wood, or a thing made of wood, appears in a deliberate sequence: the useful wood and the useless scrap carved into a god (13:11–13); the sailor's idol, more rotten than his ship (14:1); the ship, steered by God (14:3–5); the ark, "blessed" (14:7), which 10:4 had called a "worthless bit of wood" (euteles xylon) piloted by Wisdom; and the handmade image, "cursed" (14:8). Wood itself is neither holy nor evil: what matters is whether it serves God's saving purpose or is called a god. Deuteronomy 21:23 in Greek curses everyone hanged "on wood" (epi xylou), and Paul quotes it: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree" (Galatians 3:13). I suggest that the Christian reading of 14:7 as the cross drew strength from this blessed-and-cursed pair, which matches Paul's paradox. I have not found this link argued in any source opened here.

a: there will be a visitation even on the idols of the nations
p: Episkopē, "visitation", is God's coming to look into things, to judge or to save.
b: Episkopē is God's "visitation": his coming to inspect, in judgment or in rescue (3:7; 3:13; 4:15; 19:15 in this book). Here it is judgment on the idols themselves. The prophets said the same: the LORD will judge the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12; Jeremiah 46:25) and the idols will vanish (Isaiah 2:18; Zephaniah 2:11).
orig: ἐπισκοπὴ ἔσται (episkopē estai)

a: Thinking up idols was how sexual sin began
p: Porneia means sexual sin. The prophets also called idolatry Israel's unfaithfulness to God, her husband.
b: Porneia is sexual sin of any kind. The writer may mean it literally: idol worship led to sexual vice, as 14:24–26 says. He may also mean it as the prophets did, for idolatry itself as unfaithfulness to God (Hosea 1:2; Ezekiel 16; Jeremiah 3:6). The KJV adds the word "spiritual" ("the beginning of spiritual fornication"), choosing the second sense. Both senses suit the chapter, and Paul links idols and sexual sin the same way (Romans 1:24–25; Colossians 3:5).
orig: Ἀρχὴ γὰρ πορνείας ἐπίνοια εἰδώλων (archē gar porneias epinoia eidōlōn)
r: Hosea 1:2; Ezekiel 16:15; Jeremiah 3:6; Romans 1:24–25; Colossians 3:5; Revelation 2:20

a: They were not there at the start
t: Compared with the Bible: where idols came from
p: The Bible says how sin began, not how idols began. This book offers a history of idolatry.
b: Agrees with the Bible that the true God was worshiped first and idols came later: Joshua 24:2 says Israel's fathers beyond the River served other gods, and Romans 1:21–23 says people "traded the glory of the immortal God for a likeness". Goes beyond the 66 books, which give no account of how idols first arose. The book offers two: a grieving father (14:15) and the honoring of distant kings (14:17). These follow a Greek theory that the gods were once famous humans (see 14:15). Paul, by contrast, says that behind idols stand demons (1 Corinthians 10:20), a view also found in Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37. The two answers are not exclusive.

a: made an image of the child so quickly snatched away
p: The idea that gods began as honored dead people was a Greek theory, named after Euhemerus.
b: The Greek writer Euhemerus of Messene, as Lactantius reports, drew on inscriptions in ancient temples to show that Jupiter (Zeus) had been a man who reigned on earth and died; Lactantius uses him against the pagan gods (Divine Institutes 1.11). "Euhemerism" became the name for the theory that gods were humans made divine. Wisdom of Solomon gives a tender version: a father, mad with grief, makes an image of his dead child, honors it, and hands on rites to his household. Verdict: a real use of a Greek kind of theory for a Jewish argument; there is no evidence for this exact story as history.

a: made an image of him that everyone could see
p: From Alexander on, kings received divine honors, and in Egypt the Ptolemies were worshiped as gods.
b: After Alexander the Great, the kings who ruled his empire received divine honors, and in Egypt the Ptolemies were worshiped as gods; in Roman times the emperor's image stood in cities across the empire. The writer describes how it worked: distant subjects honored the king's image as if he were present. Daniel's golden statue (Daniel 3) and Revelation's image of the beast (Revelation 13:14–15) show the same fear among Jews and Christians. When the book was written is discussed in its introduction.

a: the Name that can be shared with no one
p: The Greek means the name that cannot be shared: the name "God". Aquinas quotes this verse.
b: The Greek to akoinōnēton onoma means "the name that has no partner", the name that belongs to God alone. The KJV calls it "the incommunicable name". Isaiah says, "I am the LORD; that is my name. / I will not hand my glory to another, / nor the praise owed me to carved images" (Isaiah 42:8). Thomas Aquinas quotes this verse when he asks whether the name "God" can be shared, and concludes that it is "incommunicable in reality, but communicable in opinion" (Summa Theologiae I, question 13, article 9). Whether the writer meant the word "God" or the divine name YHWH, which Greek Jews did not speak aloud, is debated.
orig: τὸ ἀκοινώνητον ὄνομα (to akoinōnēton onoma)

a: they give the name peace to evils so great
p: Jeremiah condemned those who say "Peace, peace" where there is no peace.
b: The writer calls life without God "a vast war of ignorance" that its people call peace. Jeremiah charged the prophets and priests of his day with healing the people's wound lightly, saying "Peace" when there was none (Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 8:11).

a: Everything is a mix of blood and murder, theft and deceit
p: This list of vices, 14:23–26, is the closest Jewish parallel to Paul's list in Romans 1:29–31.
b: Lists of vices were common in Greek moral writing. This one shows the writer's chain of cause and effect: false worship (14:23) leads to sexual sin and violence (14:24), and then to a breakdown of every bond (14:25–26). Paul's list in Romans 1 follows idolatry in the same way: "Every kind of unrighteousness, wickedness, greed and evil fills them. They are loaded with envy, murder, strife, deceit and spite" (Romans 1:29). Both lists name murder and deceit; both end in the loss of family love and kindness. See the note at Romans 1:29 on this site.

a: the harassing of good people
p: The Greek thorybos agathōn can mean "disturbance of good people" or "confusion about what is good".
b: Thorybos agathōn is "uproar of agathoi", and agathoi can be good people or good things. The KJV gives "Disquieting of good men" (and places it at the start of 14:26). The words can also mean "confusion about good", a moral confusion where good and evil are mixed up, which fits the next phrase, "forgetting of kindness". The Plain chooses "good people", with the KJV.
orig: θόρυβος ἀγαθῶν (thorybos agathōn)

a: the mixing up of kinds
p: Geneseōs enallagē, "exchange of kind", may mean sexual acts against nature, or confusing children's birth.
b: The Greek geneseōs enallagē is literally "exchange of genesis": of birth, origin or kind. The KJV has "changing of kind". The phrase can be taken two ways. It may mean sexual acts that exchange what is natural, as Paul says women "changed the natural use for one that goes against nature" (Romans 1:26), with a verb from the same root (metallassō). Or it may mean swapping or abandoning children, so that a family line is confused, which suits the "disorder in marriage" that follows. The Plain keeps a near-literal phrase so that readers can weigh both. The churches' views on Romans 1:26–27 are on the card at Romans 1.
orig: γενέσεως ἐναλλαγή (geneseōs enallagē)

a: idols too vile to name
p: Anōnymos means "nameless": idols not worth naming, or that must not be named.
b: The Greek anōnymōn eidōlōn may mean idols that are nothing and have no real name, or idols whose names must not be spoken. The Torah tells Israel, "Do not even mention the names of other gods" (Exodus 23:13), and Psalm 16:4 refuses to take their names on the lips. Either way, the line sets the false gods against "the Name that can be shared with no one" (14:21).
orig: ἀνωνύμων εἰδώλων (anōnymōn eidōlōn)

a: they swear falsely and do not expect to be hurt for it
p: Ancient oaths called a god to punish the one who lied. A god who is nothing cannot punish.
b: In the ancient world an oath named a god as witness and judge. If the gods are lifeless, the writer reasons, idol-worshipers can lie under oath without fear. But they will be punished anyway (14:30–31), because what punishes perjury is not the false god but the justice of the true one. The Torah forbids swearing falsely by God's name (Leviticus 19:12), and Jesus tells his followers not to swear at all (Matthew 5:33–37).

a: You are slow to anger
p: The four words come from God's self-description in Exodus 34:6.
b: "Kind and true, slow to anger, governing all with mercy" echoes the words God speaks to Moses: "a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). The Septuagint there uses makrothymos and alēthinos, close to this verse's makrothymos and alēthēs. After two chapters about false gods, the writer turns back to address the true one, in the words of Israel's oldest confession.
orig: χρηστὸς καὶ ἀληθής, μακρόθυμος (chrēstos kai alēthēs, makrothymos)

a: Even if we sin, we are yours
t: "Even if we sin, we are yours"
p: Comfort or complacency? The verse can be heard both ways.
b: The verse can be read as the confidence of a people in covenant: even when they sin, they belong to God and can return, as the prophets promised (Jeremiah 3:22; Hosea 14:1–4). It immediately adds the moral consequence: "knowing we are counted as yours, we will not sin". Read beside Romans 2, though, the first line can sound like a confidence that makes sin less serious, and Paul challenges that kind of confidence in Romans 2:1–4 and Romans 2:17–24. See the note at Romans 2:1 on this site. 1 John 2:1 holds both sides: John writes "that you not sin. Yet if someone does sin, we have an Advocate with the Father" (1 John 2:1).
r: Jeremiah 3:22; Hosea 14:1–4; Romans 2:1–4; Romans 2:17–24; Romans 6:1–2; 1 John 2:1

a: the root from which immortality grows
p: Knowing God is the root of athanasia, immortality, the book's hope for the righteous.
b: Athanasia, "immortality", is one of the book's key words (3:4; 4:1; 8:13; 8:17). Here its root is knowing God and his might, in the sense of a relationship, not information. Jesus prays, "Eternal life is this: to know you, the only real God" (John 17:3). The site keeps "immortality" (athanasia) apart from "incorruption" (aphtharsia, 2:23; 6:18–19); see the topic on the soul.
orig: ῥίζα ἀθανασίας (rhiza athanasias)

a: by painters' wasted labor
p: The Greek skiagraphos, "shadow-painter", named an artist who painted lifelike scenes with light and shade.
b: Skiagraphoi were painters who used shading to make figures look solid. The writer adds painted images to carved ones: colorful, lifelike, and still dead. Israel, he says, was not fooled by them, a claim Israel's own history makes harder to believe (Exodus 32; 2 Kings 17:7–17). The claim fits the writer's present: Jews in Alexandria were known for refusing images.
orig: σκιαγράφων πόνος ἄκαρπος (skiagraphōn ponos akarpos)

a: From the same clay he forms
p: Paul's potter in Romans 9:21 shares several Greek words with this verse.
b: The potter is an old picture of God (Isaiah 45:9; Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 18:6). Here the potter is a man who makes clean pots and unclean pots from the same clay, and then, worst of all, a god. Paul asks: "From one lump of clay, does the potter not have the authority to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" (Romans 9:21). The Greek words for potter (kerameus), clay (pēlos), the same (ek tou autou) and vessel (skeuos) appear in both. The use differs: Wisdom of Solomon mocks the potter who makes a god; Paul defends God the Potter's freedom.
orig: ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ πηλοῦ (ek tou autou pēlou)

a: when the debt of his soul is demanded back
p: Life is a loan from God, to be demanded back at death. Jesus uses the same verb in Luke 12:20.
b: The Greek says he will be "asked back the debt of his soul". Psychē here is the life itself (see terms), lent by God and called back at death, as 15:16 says the potter's breath is "on loan". In Jesus' parable, God says to the rich fool, "On this very night they demand your soul back from you" (Luke 12:20), with the same verb apaiteō. The words "go back to the earth he was taken from" follow Genesis 3:19: "until you go back to the ground, / for you were taken from it" (Genesis 3:19).
orig: τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπαιτηθεὶς χρέος (to tēs psychēs apaitētheis chreos)

a: who breathed into him a soul that acts
p: The verse retells Genesis 2:7: God shaped the man and breathed life into him.
b: Genesis 2:7 says, "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground and blew into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). The Septuagint there uses eplasen, "shaped", and enephysēsen, "blew into", the same verbs as this verse. Codices Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read "the one who made him" for "shaped" (see the variant), which loses the first of the two echoes. The writer doubles the gift: a "soul that acts" and a "life-giving breath", Greek terms that match the book's idea of the soul. The potter makes a dead thing from clay; God made a living one.
orig: ἐμφυσήσαντα πνεῦμα ζωτικόν (emphysēsanta pneuma zōtikon)

a: a fair for making money
p: The Greek panēgyrismos was a festival with a market, the kind of crowd a trader loves.
b: Panēgyrismos is a festival gathering, like the great Greek feasts, where markets did a busy trade. For the potter, life is a game and a money-making fair: idol-making is a business (compare Acts 19:24–27, where Ephesus's silversmiths riot to protect their trade in shrines of Artemis). In Swete's Codex Vaticanus the verb is singular, "he thought"; most other manuscripts and the KJV have "they thought" (see the variant).
orig: πανηγυρισμὸν ἐπικερδῆ (panēgyrismon epikerdē)

a: the enemies of your people who oppressed them
p: After the long digression, the writer returns to Egypt, the oppressor, and to its animal gods.
b: The digression on idols (13:1–15:13) ends here and the writer returns to the Exodus, where it stopped at 11:14. The "enemies of your people" are the Egyptians, whom the writer accuses of the worst idolatry: all the idols of the nations and the animals besides (15:15–18). Readers in Alexandria lived among Egyptians and Greeks who worshiped such images, and the book is one of the clearest witnesses to how a Jewish community there drew the line between itself and its neighbors.

a: yet these cannot use eyes for seeing
p: The list of useless eyes, noses, ears, hands and feet follows Psalm 115 and Psalm 135.
b: The psalm says of idols: "eyes they have, but they cannot see. / Ears they have, but they cannot hear; / a nose they have, but they cannot smell. / With their hands they cannot touch; / with their feet they cannot walk" (Psalm 115:5–7; compare Psalm 135:15–17). The writer keeps the order and adds a Greek touch: noses "for drawing breath", which links back to 15:11 and 15:16, where breath is God's gift.

a: God's praise and God's blessing have both passed them by
p: Genesis 1 says God saw what he made was good and blessed the animals. The writer says these were left out.
b: At creation God looked at what he made "and there it was, very good" (Genesis 1:31), and he blessed the creatures of the sea and air (Genesis 1:22). The writer says the animals Egypt worships, such as snakes and crocodiles, "escaped" God's praise and blessing, perhaps thinking of the snake cursed in Genesis 3:14. Compared with the Bible: Genesis says everything God made was very good; the writer does not deny this, but he singles out the creatures Egypt adored as the lowest of all. It is polemic more than natural history.
